items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that quantitative easing is an effective policy tool in a deep recession. [15]
items.answer: QE helped prevent deeper recessions, but its effect on real activity is uncertain and its distributional side effects are significant.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lowers long-term rates when policy rates are at zero; stabilises financial markets (e.g. 2008, 2020); raises asset prices and confidence. Arguments against: benefits asset holders, worsening wealth inequality; weak transmission if banks and households do not want to borrow; difficult to reverse; risk of future inflation; may create asset bubbles. Supported judgement: QE helped prevent deeper recessions, but its effect on real activity is uncertain and its distributional side effects are significant. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "political constraints on fiscal policy".
items.answer: Limits on fiscal policy arising from elections, opposition to tax rises or spending cuts, and legislative approval

items.stem: Briefly describe Argentina's currency board collapse and explain what it reveals about unsustainable fixed exchange rates.
items.answer: Argentina pegged the peso 1:1 to the US dollar under a currency board from 1991; in January 2002 it abandoned the peg and the peso lost about 70% of its value within months. Recession, debt and loss of reserves made the peg impossible to defend
items.markingKey: Context (Argentina pegged the peso 1:1 to the US dollar under a currency board from 1991; in January 2002 it abandoned the peg and the peso lost about 70% of its value within months.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Recession, debt and loss of reserves made the peg impossible to defend – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to unsustainable fixed exchange rates.

items.stem: You are an economist advising the government. A minister argues that a freely floating exchange rate is the best exchange-rate system for a small open economy. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.

Calculate the official unemployment rate and an adjusted rate that includes discouraged workers, and explain why the official rate may understate the true extent of unemployment.

items.stem: You are a policy adviser to the ministry of finance. A minister argues that deflation is more harmful to an economy than inflation. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Persistent demand-led deflation is usually more damaging than moderate inflation, which is why central banks target low positive inflation of about 2%.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: deflationary spiral reduces AD and output; increases real debt burdens; monetary policy is constrained at the zero lower bound. Counter-points: high inflation erodes savings and creates uncertainty; hyperinflation can destroy a currency; benign deflation from productivity is not harmful. Recommendation: Persistent demand-led deflation is usually more damaging than moderate inflation, which is why central banks target low positive inflation of about 2%. items.stem: You are an economist advising the government. A minister argues that high government debt is a serious threat to an economy. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: High debt is risky if it is in foreign currency, held by foreigners and rising faster than GDP; otherwise gradual stabilisation is preferable to rapid austerity.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: rising interest payments crowd out public services; risk of loss of confidence and crisis; burden on future generations. items.stem: What would shift the SRAS curve to the left?
items.answer: A rise in the price of imported raw materials
items.markingKey: A rise in the price of imported raw materials. Higher input costs reduce the output firms supply at each price level.

items.stem: With reference to China's accession to the WTO in 2001, explain how it illustrates the case for free trade.
items.answer: After joining the WTO in 2001, China's exports grew from about $270 bn in 2001 to over $3.3 trillion by 2022. Lower barriers allowed China to specialise according to comparative advantage, raising output and incomes
items.markingKey: Context (After joining the WTO in 2001, China's exports grew from about $270 bn in 2001 to over $3.3 trillion by 2022.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lower barriers allowed China to specialise according to comparative advantage, raising output and incomes – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the case for free trade.

items.stem:
Read the extract below.

Between 2010 and 2012 Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus needed financial assistance; without their own currencies they could not devalue and had to cut wages and spending.

Estonia joined the euro in 2011 despite the recent crisis and later experienced inflation above 20% in 2022, the highest in the euro area.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that the benefits of the euro have outweighed its costs for member countries.
items.answer: Benefits have been greater for open, well-synchronised economies; for periphery economies costs were large during crises, so the outcome depends on convergence and on fiscal and banking union.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: lower transaction costs and exchange risk; price transparency and competition; low inflation and credibility for previously high-inflation members; deeper capital markets. Arguments against: loss of independent monetary policy and exchange-rate adjustment; asymmetric shocks and the 2010-2012 crisis; limited fiscal transfers and labour mobility; divergence between core and periphery. Judgement: Benefits have been greater for open, well-synchronised economies; for periphery economies costs were large during crises, so the outcome depends on convergence and on fiscal and banking union. Reward explicit use of the extract. items.stem: Sofia writes: "In the Keynesian model, an increase in AD always causes inflation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: On the horizontal section of the Keynesian AS curve, higher AD increases real output without raising the price level.
items.markingKey: On the horizontal section of the Keynesian AS curve, higher AD increases real output without raising the price level. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: You are an adviser to the central bank. A minister argues that a current account deficit is always a problem for an economy. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: A deficit is a problem when it is large, persistent and financed by short-term borrowing for consumption, not when it reflects productive investment financed by FDI.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: implies growing foreign debt; may reflect lack of competitiveness; vulnerable to sudden stops of capital. Counter-points: may reflect high investment that raises future capacity; financed by FDI is more sustainable; USA has run deficits for decades. Recommendation: A deficit is a problem when it is large, persistent and financed by short-term borrowing for consumption, not when it reflects productive investment financed by FDI.
